rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The predicate of “those confederates” is omitted because the context and following clause make their fate evident.
rows.anchor: This is because it is self-evident from the occasion and context and the next part of the verse is pointing to it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prominent nations were routed when punishment came; the Quraysh will meet the same fate if they follow their ways.
rows.anchor: look at the fate these prominent nations; when the punishment of God arrived they were totally routed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each nation’s crime was rejecting its messenger, and the Quraysh are now guilty of the same crime.
rows.anchor: the crime of each of these nations was that they rejected their respective messenger and the Quraysh too are now guilty of this crime.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “ḥaqqa ʿiqāb,” the yāʾ of “ʿiqābī” is omitted for the passage’s rhyme, as in 38:8.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word “fawāq” means respite.
rows.anchor: The word ٍاقَوَف means “respite”.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh demand punishment arrogantly, but one divine blast will rout them and they will not escape it even briefly.
rows.anchor: only one shout of God will be needed to rout them; a second one would not even be required.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word “qiṭṭ” means share.
rows.anchor: The word َّطِق means “share”.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh demanded punishment before Judgement Day to test Muḥammad’s claim; the author links their demand to the one in al-Anfāl.
rows.anchor: This demand of the Quraysh is also mentioned in Sūrah Anfāl in the following words:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an is a great favour: receptive people are moved by it, while the stone-hearted are deprived of it and face destruction like messenger-denying nations.
rows.anchor: The stone-hearted, however, will be deprived from the Qur’ān and will face the punishment of destruction

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an presents all facts in the best style; its opponents will be taken to task, while those accepting its truth fear God and receive the best reward.
rows.anchor: The Qur’ān has delineated all the facts in the best of styles. Those who are opposing it will be taken to task.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s warning about the rejecters’ fate seems far-fetched to them.
rows.anchor: This verse reminds the rejecters of the Qur’ān that the fate the Prophet (sws) is warning them of at that time seems far-fetched to them;

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh’s success intoxicates them, so they cannot imagine their dominance ending even as they witness the world’s mortality.
rows.anchor: intoxicated with their success that they cannot think from where their dominance would see its doom even though they are continuously witnessing the fact that everything of this world is temporary and mortal.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Alwān” can also mean types.
rows.anchor: The word  انَوْلَأُ also means “types”.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression “hāja al-nabāt” means that the vegetation started to dry out.
rows.anchor: the vegetation started to dry out

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The observation of this cycle is a great lesson for people of understanding.
rows.anchor: there is a great lesson for men of understanding in this observation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because life’s pleasures are temporary, an intelligent person should turn toward the self-sufficient Creator who brought them into existence.
rows.anchor: a person of intellect should direct his attention to the Being Who brought all these things into existence and is not dependent on any thing for His existence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People owe gratitude to their Lord for providing their sustenance and should not direct that gratitude to others.
rows.anchor: it is the natural obligation of people to thank their Lord Who made this arrangement in this world for their sustenance and nourishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Creator will hold each person accountable and reward or punish them according to justice.
rows.anchor: there must come a day in which He will hold each person accountable for his good and evil deeds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As with rain on land, the Qur’an benefits people according to their capacities: receptive hearts flourish, while those hardened after wasting their abilities remain barren and face doom.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s parts are uniform in their basic teachings, though its groups and sūrahs differ in style and central themes; this unity manifests its majesty.

rows.claim: This form of revelation serves teaching by letting readers observe the facts to which the Qur’an invites them from several angles.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Mathānī” refers to the Qur’anic sūrahs occurring in pairs, a reading discussed at 15:87 and valued for teaching.
rows.anchor: this word refers to the occurrence of the Qur’ānic sūrahs in pairs.

rows.speaker: People who think that the word means “something which is repeated often”
rows.claim: The author rejects the view that “mathānī” means something often repeated, calling it contrary to linguistic principles and parallel constructions.
rows.anchor: People who think that the word means “something which is repeated often” are mistaken and their view is against linguistic principles and parallel constructions.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Julūd” can mean the body’s skin or hair, with Arabic using a part for the whole and the whole for a part.
rows.anchor: The word ُودُلُج means the hair on the skin of the body as well as the body itself.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because “talīnu” is followed by “ilā,” it includes the sense of inclining toward.
rows.anchor: Since the word  ُنیِلَت is followed by the preposition  ىَلِإِit encompasses the meaning of لْیِمَت inclined to).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s sūrahs differ while refreshing one another’s themes; the Torah’s successive books lack such connection, a discontinuity related to its loss or alteration.
rows.anchor: On the other hand, the case of the Torah is very different.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an so profoundly affects those who fear God that their hairs stand on end; lack of effect signals a heart devoid of God’s light and hardened.
rows.anchor: the hairs on their skins stand on their ends.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s softening makes bodies and hearts tender and turn toward God.
rows.anchor: induces their bodies and hearts to become tender and turn towards God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bodily tenderness means that no arrogance or haughtiness remains.
rows.anchor: what is implied by the tenderness of the bodies is that no speck of arrogance and haughtiness remains in them.
